strengths: Well-motivated problem: label noise in preference datasets is a real and practically important issue for RLHF/DPO-style alignment, supported by citations quantifying its prevalence and impact.

General and elegant unifying framework: the Gibbs/Boltzmann construction (Eq. 2) links a broad class of preference losses (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO) to induced probabilistic models, allowing a single EM-based robustification scheme to be applied across algorithms rather than proposing a loss specific to one method.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 proves that, under an idealized (perfectly calibrated, population-level) setting, the EM reliability updates converge to the true annotator reliability; the paper is transparent that this is an idealized guarantee and discusses its limitations honestly.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: two backbones (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), four alignment objectives, two benchmarks (AlpacaEval2, Arena-Hard), a real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with genuine annotator disagreement, and comparisons to label smoothing, rDPO, and Holder-DPO baselines.

Good ancillary analyses: qualitative case studies showing intuitively sensible low-confidence examples, ablations on prior η0 and EMA momentum, synthetic noise-injection experiments that empirically corroborate the convergence theorem, annotator reliability histograms on MultiPref, and a runtime overhead analysis (a nice touch for practical adoption).
Reasonable reproducibility effort: derivations for the EM steps and theorem are given in appendices, and links to models/datasets are provided.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are inconsistent across algorithm families: for CPO on Mistral-7B, RE-PO (27.6/27.8) underperforms simple label smoothing (28.5/28.8); for SimPO on Llama-3-8B, RE-PO's LC score (46.9) is lower than label smoothing (48.1). This undercuts the claim that RE-PO is uniformly superior to a trivial baseline, and the paper's framing ("generally enhances") somewhat glosses over these mixed results.

In the main UltraFeedback experiments, the paper collapses all annotators into a single virtual annotator (K=1), which substantially weakens the core motivating idea of modeling heterogeneous annotator reliability — in this setting the EM reduces to estimating a single global noise/confidence weight per example rather than truly leveraging the annotator-reliability latent structure that is the paper's main theoretical selling point. The more faithful multi-annotator test (MultiPref) is only run with DPO/RE-DPO, not the other three algorithm families.

No variance/error bars are reported for the main results in Table 2 (unlike the ablation table), making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., +7.0 pts) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise, especially given AlpacaEval2's known evaluation variance.

Missing comparisons to other closely related robust-preference-optimization baselines explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., ROPO, Selective DPO), which would strengthen the empirical positioning beyond rDPO and Holder-DPO.

Non-trivial computational overhead (average ~11%, up to ~40% for SimPO) is disclosed but not deeply analyzed or mitigated, and it is unclear how this overhead scales with dataset size/number of annotators in more realistic large-K settings.

The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.1) relies on strong idealized assumptions (perfect calibration, full-batch/population level, converged M-step) that are quite far from the practical mini-batch/EMA implementation actually used; while the paper acknowledges this gap and provides some empirical support, the disconnect between theory and the deployed algorithm remains a limitation.

Evaluation is limited to AlpacaEval2/Arena-Hard-style instruction-following win-rate metrics; there is no assessment of whether the noise-robust reweighting affects other capabilities (e.g., reasoning, knowledge benchmarks, safety) or introduces unintended biases from down-weighting legitimately difficult-but-correct examples versus truly noisy ones.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: label noise in preference data used for LLM alignment.

The core methodological contribution—connecting arbitrary preference losses to a Gibbs/Bradley-Terry-style probabilistic model via Eq. (2)—is elegant and enables RE-PO to be applied as a plug-in to DPO, IPO, SimPO, and CPO with minimal modification, giving the work genuine 'general framework' status rather than being a single-algorithm proposal.

A convergence theorem (Theorem 4.1) is provided with a full derivation in the appendix, showing that under a perfectly calibrated model the EM annotator-reliability updates converge to the true reliability; this is a nontrivial theoretical contribution beyond typical engineering-style robustness papers.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: two backbones (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), four alignment algorithms, AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard benchmarks, a real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with per-annotator reliability modeling, hyperparameter ablations, synthetic noise-recovery experiments validating the theorem, and a wall-clock runtime overhead analysis.
Comparisons against reasonable and relevant baselines (label smoothing, rDPO, Hölder-DPO) are included, and RE-PO is shown to outperform them in most settings.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix F) convincingly illustrate that low-confidence weights assigned by RE-PO correspond to genuinely noisy/reversed preference labels, supporting the mechanism's face validity.
Good reproducibility support: derivations, algorithm pseudocode, dataset/model links, and additional judge-robustness checks (DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Main results in Table 2 report no variance across seeds or repeated runs, despite AlpacaEval 2/Arena-Hard being known to have appreciable evaluation noise; several reported gains (e.g., 1-2 point differences) may not be statistically distinguishable from baselines or from label smoothing, weakening the strength of the 'consistent improvement' claim.

The 'consistently enhances' framing is somewhat overstated: in at least two family/backbone combinations (CPO on Mistral-7B, SimPO on Llama-3-8B) plain label smoothing actually matches or outperforms RE-PO, which is not adequately discussed as a limitation.

Theorem 4.1's guarantee relies on a 'perfectly calibrated model' assumption that is acknowledged as unrealistic; while synthetic experiments partially support robustness to miscalibration, no formal bound or guarantee is given for the more realistic case of an imperfectly calibrated policy, so the theoretical contribution's practical implications remain limited.

For the UltraFeedback-based main experiments, multiple annotators are collapsed into a single 'virtual annotator' (K=1), which removes exactly the per-annotator structure that motivates the Dawid-Skene-style EM design; this simplification is not deeply analyzed for how much it affects the denoising benefit versus a simpler per-example-only noise model.

It is unclear whether the actual datasets used contain substantial label noise as claimed (citing Gao et al.'s 20-40% estimate for general datasets), so it is hard to disentangle whether RE-PO's gains stem from genuine noise correction versus a general regularization/smoothing effect similar to label smoothing (which the paper's own results partially suggest, since LS is sometimes competitive).

The generalization step (Eq. 2) applying the Gibbs-distribution trick to arbitrary losses (e.g., CPO, which includes an additional non-pairwise NLL term) is not rigorously justified for losses that are not simple functions of a signed margin; the probabilistic interpretation for CPO in particular deserves more careful treatment, since CPO's implicit reward structure differs from a pure Bradley-Terry-style formulation.

The runtime overhead analysis (up to ~20%, sometimes non-monotonic/negative in some configurations) is reported but not deeply investigated, leaving open questions about scalability to larger annotator pools or larger-scale training runs.

The paper would benefit from testing on additional/larger-scale preference datasets beyond the two UltraFeedback variants and MultiPref to more convincingly establish generality of the robustness claims.
